caseno: Criminal Appeal No. 443 of 1995 with Criminal Appeal No. 232 of 1995
lawyer:
Md Khurshid Alam Khan with Ahmed Ali and Md Salahuddin Talukder; Advocates ----- For the Accused-Appellants
KM Saifuddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General with Mahmood Hossain, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For the Respondent-State.
parties:
Shah Alam and others ------ Petitioners
vs
State ------ Respondent
full_judgment: 18. Mr KM Saifuddin Ahmed, learned Deputy Attorney-General, submits with loud voice that the examination of recording Magistrate is not necessary and in support of his submission he referred to a decision in the case of Abul Khayer and three others vs State reported in 46 DLR 212. We have gone through the same minutely and have reasons to believe that the learned Deputy Attorney-General hits failed to digest the findings and decision arrived at in the aforesaid rulings. Be the case as it may, the learned Advocate for the appellants referred to a decision in the case of Babul alias Abdul Majid Khan and others is State reported in 42 DLR(AD) 186, wherein it has been held that even there is provision for making certain presumption in respect of the confession by an accused person produced before a Court taken in accordance with law and purporting to be signed by a Magistrate having regard to the facts of the case it with injudicious to rely upon such confession without calling the Magistrate as a witness. In ie4pect of confession the Court is required to see not only that the forms under sections 164 and 364 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were complied with but the substance underneath the law was equally adhered to there must not be any reason for doubt as to the truth of the statements, be it circumstance or proved otherwise. In this particular case it is difficult to deny accused-appellants an opportunity to cross-examine the Magistrate who allegedly recorded their statements. This view has been supported by a decision in the case of Ustar Ali vs the State reported in 18 BLD (AD) 43 = 3 BLC (AD) 53. Coupled with this we may be permitted to refer to the evidence of PW 11 wherein she admitted that her colleague recorded the confessional statements of accused Shah Alum and Ali Mia and that thereafter the confessing accused were again given on remand as per prayer of the Investigating Officer. Giving of remand of the confessing accused after recording his confessional statements is against the principle of law and it has been held that the order of remand after recording the confessional statement of concerned accused is not in accordance With law inasmuch as the same is illegal and, as such, the prosecution cannot get any benefit out of the confessional statements of these two accused, namely, Shah Alam and Ali Mia. So, it appears that the confessional statements of accused-appellant Shah Alam and Ali Mia (not appellant before us) Exhibits-7 and 8 respectively are not in accordance with law and, as such, the same cannot form the basis of conviction. As regards the confessional statements of accused-appellants Selim Choudhury and Ashat Ali Exhibits-5 and 6 respectively recorded by PW 11 the less said the better, because these are inadmissible in evidence, since the alleged confessing accused were handed over for further remand after recording their confessional statement as admitted by the recording Magistrate PW 11. So, it appears that the alleged confessional statements of accused persons. namely, Shah Alum, Selim Choudhury, and Ashat Ali and accused Ali Mia (not appellant before us) cannot be regarded as confessional statements within the meaning of sections 164 and 364 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, as such, the prosecution in no way can get any support therefrom. In this connection we may recall here that there is no doubt of oral evidence regarding the accused-appellant Kiwi Shahjahan. The oral evidence is practically nil and that no incriminating article was recovered from his possession and that he neither confessed his guilt nor produced in TI parade. The only evidence against him is that confessing accused persons implicated him in the matter of commission of dacoity in question. Since we have already found earlier that the alleged confession of the aforesaid confessing accused are not in accordance with law inasmuch as the same are not admissible in evidence, accused-appellant Kazi Shahjahan cannot be held guilty for the offence charged under section 395 of the Penal Code on the basis of co-accused who made confessional statements and the same being found illegal, he also cannot be convicted on the basis thereof.
